description: We are people who can do something impressive immediately.
summary:
We built Space_MarS, an open-source web engine that helps farmers choose crop rotations that survive extreme weather.

Our tool turns 40 years of daily NASA POWER weather data (1984–2026) into field-level financial risk estimates. Coupling NASA reanalysis with FAO soil water balance and yield response models (FAO-56 and FAO-33), the engine runs 10,000 Monte Carlo climate futures directly in the browser in about one second. A farmer selects their official parcel boundary via land registry or tractor GPS, sets their soil type and local buyer prices, and gets plain numbers in local currency: expected profit, bad-year downside, seed orders, and subsidy totals.

By connecting satellite climatology directly to field-level economics, Space_MarS turns climate resilience into a straightforward business decision
details:
Farmers around the world face increasingly volatile weather, yet most crop rotation choices are still made by habit or based on whatever grain fetched a good price the previous autumn. Existing climate tools tend to produce abstract maps showing temperature anomalies decades into the future, which is useless for a grower who has to decide what seeds to buy this month. On typical arable land in Central Europe, continuing with a standard cereal and maize rotation leads to a financial loss in one out of every three years, and in a severe drought year that loss can exceed thirteen hundred zlotys per hectare. We built Space MarS to solve this gap by turning forty years of satellite climate observations into direct, field-level financial risk numbers.

The tool works directly in the browser and requires under a minute to evaluate a farm. A user starts by selecting their exact parcel boundary, which can be pulled live from national land registry APIs, drawn on a three-dimensional terrain map, or grabbed instantly via phone GPS while sitting in the tractor. The farmer then selects their soil profile from seven standard agricultural classes and enters local grain elevator prices. Under the hood, the engine downloads forty years of daily NASA POWER weather data, spanning from 1984 to 2026, including precipitation, daily temperature extremes, solar radiation, humidity, and wind speed. We run a daily water balance based on the FAO-56 dual crop coefficient method to track root-zone soil moisture and storm runoff, and calculate yield penalties using FAO-33 crop sensitivity across vegetative, flowering, and ripening stages. We also layered in explicit hazard models for spring frost events during flowering and excessive rainfall during harvest windows, which cause grain quality downgrades.

Rather than assuming an average year, our engine runs a Monte Carlo simulation of ten thousand synthetic seasons. It cross-samples historical weather patterns with correlated commodity price shocks and current European Union eco-scheme subsidies. The entire computation runs client-side using JavaScript Web Workers in about one second. The output gives the farmer clear financial metrics instead of academic jargon. For example, our simulations demonstrate that replacing a cereal monoculture with a diversified rotation of soy, winter wheat, sunflower, and rye reduces worst-case drought losses from thirteen hundred zlotys down to just ninety-six zlotys per hectare, while more than tripling average multi-year profit. The platform also delivers concrete operational outputs, including exact seed seeding rates per hectare, nitrogen fertilizer credits saved after growing legumes, and slope erosion warnings calculated from digital elevation models.

What makes our project distinct is that it bridges high-altitude space data with the gritty realities of everyday farm management. We designed the interface specifically for field conditions with large touch targets and built the application as an offline progressive web app. Once weather data is fetched for a location, the entire engine continues running without an internet connection, which is essential because mobile coverage often drops in rural fields. The codebase is written entirely in pure modern vanilla JavaScript with no third-party frameworks, keeping it lightweight and fast. The map uses Mapbox GL with terrain rasters and falls back to Leaflet if needed. We validated our yield response curves against twenty-five years of official Polish regional crop statistics, achieving strong correlations of zero point seventy-eight for maize and zero point seventy for wheat. We also took care to remain scientifically honest about limitations. While NASA POWER provides weather on a fifty-kilometer grid, we capture field-level differences through soil water capacity, parcel slope, and elevation, while openly flagging crops with shorter regional historical records. By keeping the entire application static with zero recurring cloud hosting costs, we ensure Space MarS remains permanently free and accessible to farmers long after the hackathon ends.
